topic: The Secret Symmetry: Euler's Characteristic and Planar Graph Duality
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Mathematics

outline.topic: The Secret Symmetry: Euler's Characteristic and Planar Graph Duality
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisites: Anatomy of a Planar Graph
sections.content: Define a planar graph as a network of points (Vertices) and lines (Edges) that can be drawn on a flat surface without any edges crossing. Introduce the concept of 'Faces'—the regions enclosed by edges, including the infinite 'outer face'. Use a simple house-shaped graph to label V, E, and F.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Spider's Web' (a simple grid). Count: Vertices (junctions), Edges (silk lines), and Faces (the gaps where flies get caught).

sections.title: The Magic Constant: Euler's Characteristic Formula
sections.content: Introduce the formula V - E + F = 2. Explain that for any connected planar graph, this value is invariant. Demonstrate the formula's robustness by 'deforming' the graph (stretching edges like rubber bands) to show that as long as edges don't cross, the result remains 2.
sections.example: Take a cube projected onto a 2D plane (Schlegel diagram). Count V=8, E=12, F=6. Calculation: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2.

sections.title: Entering the Mirror Dimension: Concept of Duality
sections.content: Introduce the 'Dual Graph' construction. Step 1: Place a new vertex in the center of every face of the original graph (the 'Primal'). Step 2: Draw a new edge across every original edge to connect the vertices in adjacent faces. This creates a new graph (the 'Dual').
sections.example: An animation showing a 'Castle' graph (Primal). A 'Ghost' character places a beacon in every room and one outside. The 'Ghost' then draws paths between beacons by passing through every wall (edge).

sections.title: The Symmetry Swap: Relationships between Primal and Dual
sections.content: Analyze the mathematical transformation. The number of Vertices in the Dual (V*) equals the number of Faces in the Primal (F). The number of Faces in the Dual (F*) equals the number of Vertices in the Primal (V). The number of Edges remains identical (E* = E). Show how Euler's formula holds for both.
sections.example: Side-by-side comparison table: Primal Graph (V: 4, E: 6, F: 4) vs. Dual Graph (V*: 4, E*: 6, F*: 4). Use a Tetrahedron to demonstrate a 'Self-Dual' graph.

sections.title: Application: Why Duality Matters
sections.content: Explain that duality allows us to solve complex problems by looking at them from the opposite perspective. In circuit design or map coloring, a difficult problem regarding 'Faces' can be solved as a simpler problem regarding 'Vertices' in the dual graph.
sections.example: A 'Robot' navigating a maze. Instead of the robot avoiding walls (Edges), the robot's logic is simplified by moving between the centers of open spaces (Vertices of the Dual graph).

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: Anatomy of a Planar Graph
lecture_lines: Planar graphs are drawn without crossing edges.
They consist of vertices, edges, and faces.
Every graph includes an infinite outer face.
animations: Display a simple house-shaped graph with vertices at junctions and edges as walls. Color vertices #00FFFF, edges #FFFFFF.
Highlight the enclosed regions (Faces) one by one in #FFFF00 and then highlight the infinite outer area.
Label the counts: V=5, E=6, F=3 (including the outer face) using #FFFFFF text next to the graph.

storyboard.title: The Magic Constant: Euler's Characteristic Formula
lecture_lines: For connected planar graphs, V minus E plus F equals 2.
Let's count the vertices, edges, and faces.
Eight vertices minus twelve edges plus six faces equals two.
Stretching the graph doesn't change this constant.
This invariant is called the Euler characteristic.
animations: Display the formula "V - E + F = 2" in large #FFFFFF text at the top.
Show a 2D projection of a cube (Schlegel diagram). Vertices #00FFFF, Edges #FFFFFF, Faces #FFFF00.
Label V=8, E=12, F=6. Move these values into the formula: 8 - 12 + 6.
Animate the calculation 8 - 12 + 6 = 2, flashing the "2" in #00FF00 for emphasis.
Stretch the cube's vertices like rubber bands to deform the shape, while the formula values and result remain fixed.

storyboard.title: Entering the Mirror Dimension: Concept of Duality
lecture_lines: Every planar graph has a hidden dual graph.
Place a new vertex inside every face.
Connect vertices if their faces share an edge.
These new connections form the dual edges.
The dual graph mirrors the original structure.
animations: Display a simple "Primal" graph (a triangle with a line inside) in #FFFFFF.
Place new vertices (Dual Vertices) in the center of every face (including the outer face) in #FF00FF.
For every original edge, draw a new perpendicular edge in #FF00FF connecting the Dual Vertices in the adjacent faces.
Fade out the original "Primal" graph edges and vertices, leaving only the "Dual" graph in #FF00FF.
Pulse the entire Dual graph to show it is a complete, new network.

storyboard.title: The Symmetry Swap: Relationships between Primal and Dual
lecture_lines: Dual vertices equal the number of original faces.
Dual faces equal the number of original vertices.
Both graphs share the same number of edges.
Euler's formula holds true for both versions.
Some special graphs are even self-dual.
animations: Show a Primal graph (left) and its Dual graph (right). Primal #FFFFFF, Dual #FF00FF.
Highlight Primal Faces and Dual Vertices simultaneously to show V* = F. Label in #FFFFFF.
Highlight Primal Vertices and Dual Faces simultaneously to show F* = V. Label in #FFFFFF.
Highlight Primal Edges and Dual Edges to show E* = E. Label in #FFFFFF.
Display a Tetrahedron graph and its dual, showing they are identical (Self-Dual), with a "Self-Dual" label in #00FF00.

storyboard.title: Application: Why Duality Matters
lecture_lines: Duality simplifies complex geometric problems.
Problems about faces become problems about vertices.
This symmetry reveals the deep structure of networks.
animations: Show a complex maze representing a "Face" problem. Color the walls (edges) #FFFFFF.
Transform the maze into its dual graph, where "Rooms" become "Vertices" and "Passages" become "Edges" in #FF00FF.
Animate a simple path through the dual vertices to demonstrate solving the problem in the dual space.
